lead: This unit explains how an analog message becomes a stream of bits. You will sample bandlimited signals without aliasing, compare PAM, PWM and PPM, design uniform and companded quantizers, and follow PCM, DPCM, ADPCM and delta modulation through TDM to line coding. After it you can compute Nyquist rates, PCM bit rates, quantization SNR, TDM frame rates and first-null line-code bandwidths.
about: This unit moves from sampling a continuous signal to sending the resulting numbers as pulses. Chapter 4.1 gives the sampling theorem, aliasing and reconstruction. Chapter 4.2 describes analog pulse modulation: PAM, PWM and PPM. Chapter 4.3 explains uniform and non-uniform quantization and companding. Chapter 4.4 builds PCM from sampling, quantization and binary encoding. Chapter 4.5 and 4.6 reduce bit rate with differential PCM and delta modulation. Chapter 4.7 packs several PCM signals into time slots with TDM. Chapter 4.8 maps the final bit stream to voltages using NRZ, RZ and Manchester line codes. The chapters build in that order: every later block takes the sampled or quantized output of an earlier one.

chapters.idea: A lowpass signal with highest frequency fm can be rebuilt exactly from samples taken at fs ≥ 2fm; sampling below that folds high frequencies onto low ones as aliasing.
chapters.depth: State and prove the sampling theorem for lowpass signals. Define sampling rate fs (samples per second), sampling interval Ts = 1/fs, Nyquist rate 2fm and Nyquist interval 1/(2fm). Derive the spectrum of ideal impulse-sampled signal: replicas of M(f) centred at kfs, spacing fs. Explain the anti-alias lowpass filter before the sampler. Show aliasing calculation: a component at f0 sampled at fs appears at |f0 − kfs| inside 0 to fs/2. Cover ideal sinc reconstruction and zero-order-hold (flat-top) reconstruction with aperture effect; natural sampling and flat-top sampling names. Mention bandpass sampling only as a note: choose fs so shifted bands do not overlap; some syllabi call the theorem Nyquist–Shannon or Whittaker. Keep proofs short; exam wants spectrum sketches and numerical alias finding.

figure.title: Spectrum when fs = 7 kHz
figure.aria: The plot shows original tones at 1 and 4 kHz, a folded 4 kHz tone at 3 kHz, and sample replicas at 6, 8 and 11 kHz for fs = 7 kHz.

chapters.example: A signal m(t) = 3 cos(2π·1000t) + 2 cos(2π·4000t) is sampled at fs = 7 kHz. Find the Nyquist rate, decide whether aliasing occurs, and give the alias frequency of the 4 kHz tone. Answer: fm = 4 kHz, Nyquist rate = 8 kHz; fs = 7 kHz < 8 kHz, so aliasing occurs; the 4 kHz tone folds to |4 − 7| = 3 kHz. The 1 kHz tone remains at 1 kHz.
chapters.trap: Do not call fs = 2fm sufficient in practice: an ideal brick-wall filter is needed; real systems use fs > 2fm with a guard band. For alias, fold into 0 to fs/2; do not simply subtract only once if f0 > fs.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: Fourier transform, bandwidth and spectra.
chapters.leave: Quantization, coding and pulse shapes to Chapters 4.3–4.4 and Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Analog pulse modulation carries the message in the amplitude, width or position of a periodic pulse; PAM varies amplitude, PWM varies width, PPM varies position.
chapters.depth: Define pulse train with period Ts and pulse width τ. PAM: sample-and-hold, natural and flat-top PAM, spectrum, aperture effect; PAM is analog until quantized. PWM (pulse-duration modulation, PDM): constant amplitude, duty cycle varies with m(t); demodulate by lowpass. PPM: constant width, leading or trailing edge shifted; generated from PWM by edge detection; larger bandwidth than PWM. Compare noise immunity: PPM/PWM constant amplitude better than PAM; bandwidth order PPM > PWM > PAM (approximately). Include PAM-TDM idea only as lead-in to Chapter 4.7. Some syllabi call PPM pulse-position modulation and PWM pulse-duration modulation.

figure.title: From message to PAM, PWM, PPM
figure.aria: A common message drives a sampler to make PAM, and a comparator with a sawtooth to make PWM; an edge detector then turns PWM into PPM.

chapters.example: A 1 kHz tone is sampled at 8 kHz. Each flat-top PAM pulse is 25 μs wide. Find the sampling interval, duty cycle, and the first null of the pulse spectrum. Answer: Ts = 1/8000 = 125 μs; duty = 25/125 = 0.20 = 20%; first null = 1/τ = 1/(25×10⁻⁶ s) = 40 kHz.
chapters.trap: PAM is not digital PCM. PWM and PPM keep constant pulse amplitude, so they are less affected by amplitude noise but need more bandwidth. PPM shifts position; do not draw it as width modulation.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 sampling; Unit 1 Fourier series and spectra.
chapters.leave: Quantization and binary coding to Chapters 4.3–4.4; TDM to Chapter 4.7.

chapters.idea: Quantization replaces each sample by one of L levels; uniform steps give fixed error power Δ²/12, while non-uniform steps and companding give small signals finer steps and more uniform SNR.
chapters.depth: Uniform quantizer with step Δ and L = 2ⁿ levels; quantization error e lies in [−Δ/2, Δ/2]; noise power Δ²/12; SQNR for full-scale sinusoid 6.02n + 1.76 dB; overload and granular distortion. Non-uniform quantization: finer steps near zero, coarser at large amplitude; companding = compressing before transmission and expanding after reception. μ-law with μ = 255 and A-law with A = 87.6 for speech; segmented approximations used in PCM. Define companding, compander, idle-channel noise. Some syllabi call non-uniform quantization logarithmic quantization or companded PCM.

figure.title: Positive half of μ-law companding
figure.aria: The plot compares a straight uniform quantizer curve with the compressed μ-law curve for μ = 255.

chapters.example: An 8-bit uniform PCM system has a full-scale sinusoidal input. Find the number of levels, step size for a ±1 V range, quantization noise power, and SQNR. Answer: L = 2⁸ = 256; Δ = 2 V/256 = 7.8125 mV; noise power = Δ²/12 = 5.09×10⁻⁶ V²; SQNR = 6.02×8 + 1.76 = 49.9 dB.
chapters.trap: 6.02n + 1.76 dB assumes a full-scale sine wave; for speech or arbitrary signals use the actual signal power. Companding improves small-signal SNR but cannot remove overload at peaks. Δ²/12 is quantization noise only; it is not total channel noise.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 sampling; Unit 1 random variables and noise power.
chapters.leave: PCM encoding to Chapter 4.4; DPCM and delta modulation to Chapters 4.5–4.6; source coding to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: PCM turns each quantized sample into an n-bit code word, so bit rate is fs·n and speech at 8 kHz with 8 bits gives 64 kbit/s.
chapters.depth: Draw PCM chain: anti-alias LPF, sampler, quantizer, encoder, channel with regenerator, decoder, reconstruction LPF. Define code word, bit duration Tb = 1/Rb, bit rate Rb = fs n, quantization levels L = 2ⁿ. Minimum baseband bandwidth Rb/2 for ideal Nyquist; first-null NRZ bandwidth Rb; practical PCM bandwidth. Quantization SNR and effect of channel noise: regenerator removes noise between repeated pulses, but bit errors add. Mention companded PCM for speech (8-bit, 8 kHz, 64 kbit/s). Synchronization word and frame only as lead-in to TDM. Some syllabi call this pulse-code modulation and include destination SNR in PCM with noise; keep that to a short block-level treatment, not a long derivation.

figure.title: PCM chain for 8 kHz, 8-bit speech
figure.aria: The PCM chain filters the message, samples it at 8 kHz, quantizes to 256 levels, encodes 8 bits per sample, sends it through a regenerator channel, then decodes and lowpass-filters the output.

chapters.example: Telephone speech is bandlimited to 3.4 kHz and sampled at 8 kHz with 8 bits per sample. Find the bit rate, minimum ideal baseband bandwidth, number of levels, and SQNR for a full-scale sine. Answer: Rb = 8000×8 = 64,000 bit/s = 64 kbit/s; minimum bandwidth = Rb/2 = 32 kHz; L = 2⁸ = 256; SQNR = 6.02×8 + 1.76 = 49.9 dB.
chapters.trap: Do not write PCM bandwidth = 8 kHz or 64 kHz automatically. 64 kbit/s is bit rate; ideal minimum baseband bandwidth is 32 kHz. Regeneration does not correct bit errors; it only reshapes pulses.
chapters.leave: Differential coding to 4.5, delta modulation to 4.6, TDM frame structure to 4.7, line codes to 4.8, channel coding to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: DPCM encodes the difference between a sample and a prediction from past samples, so correlated signals need fewer bits; ADPCM changes the quantizer step or predictor to match the signal.
chapters.depth: DPCM transmitter: predictor, subtractor, quantizer, encoder; receiver: decoder, predictor, adder. Both predictors use reconstructed past samples to avoid drift. Predictor x̂[n] = x[n−1] or a linear sum. For first-order correlation ρ, prediction error power 2σ²(1−ρ); DPCM gain over PCM at same bits = 10 log₁₀[1/(2(1−ρ))] dB. ADPCM: adapt step size from short-term signal energy; standard speech ADPCM at 32 kbit/s from 64 kbit/s PCM. Some syllabi call it differential pulse-code modulation (DPCM) and adaptive differential pulse-code modulation (ADPCM).

figure.title: DPCM with closed-loop predictor
figure.aria: The DPCM diagram subtracts a prediction from the input, quantizes and encodes the error, and feeds the reconstructed past sample back through the predictor to both subtractor and adder.

chapters.example: A first-order Markov source has variance σ² = 1 V² and adjacent-sample correlation ρ = 0.9. DPCM uses x̂[n] = x[n−1]. Find the prediction-error variance and the DPCM gain over PCM at the same number of bits. Answer: σ_e² = 2σ²(1−ρ) = 2×1×(1−0.9) = 0.2 V²; gain = 10 log₁₀(1/0.2) = 6.99 dB ≈ 7 dB.
chapters.trap: The transmitter predictor must use the same reconstructed past samples as the receiver; using the true input causes mismatch and error growth. DPCM is not delta modulation: DPCM can use many bits per difference. ADPCM adaptation is not the same as companding, though both help small signals.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.3–4.4 quantization and PCM; Unit 1 correlation.
chapters.leave: One-bit DPCM (delta modulation) to 4.6; speech coding standards details to later study; channel errors to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Delta modulation sends one bit per sample: it moves a staircase up or down by a fixed step to follow the signal; adaptive delta modulation changes the step to reduce slope overload and granular noise.
chapters.depth: DM modulator with comparator, sampler/clock, integrator; receiver integrator and lowpass. Output bit rate = fs. Step size Δ, maximum staircase slope Δfs; slope overload when |dm/dt|max > Δfs; granular noise when Δ too large. For sinusoid A sin(2πft), slope-overload condition Δfs ≥ 2πfA. ADM: step size increased after runs of equal bits, decreased after alternation; constant SNR over wide amplitude range. Compare DM/ADM with PCM: simple, low bit rate, but higher quantization noise and bandwidth. Some syllabi call DM delta modulation and ADM adaptive delta modulation.

figure.title: Delta modulator
figure.aria: The delta modulator compares the input with an integrator staircase, samples the comparator decision into one bit per sample, and feeds the bit back through the step-size integrator.

chapters.example: A 1 kHz sinusoid of amplitude 2 V is encoded by DM with step Δ = 0.1 V and sampling rate fs = 32 kHz. Check slope overload. Answer: required maximum slope = 2πfA = 2π×1000×2 = 12,566 V/s; DM maximum slope = Δfs = 0.1×32,000 = 3,200 V/s. Since 12,566 > 3,200 V/s, slope overload occurs. To avoid it, fs must be at least 12,566/0.1 = 125,660 Hz (about 126 kHz).
chapters.trap: DM bit rate is fs, not fs×n. A larger step reduces slope overload but increases granular noise; ADM trades both by adapting Δ. Do not confuse the integrator staircase with PCM reconstruction.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.5 DPCM; Chapter 4.1 sampling; Unit 1 sinusoid slope.
chapters.leave: PCM/DPCM bit-rate comparison to 4.4–4.5; TDM to 4.7; line coding to 4.8.

chapters.idea: TDM lets several signals share one link by giving each signal its own repeating time slot in a frame.
chapters.depth: TDM with PAM and PCM; frame, slot, guard time, synchronization bit or word. Frame duration Tf = 1/fs (one sample per channel per frame). For N equal channels with n bits per sample and S sync bits per frame, bit rate Rb = (N n + S) fs. Interleaving by sample or by bit/word. Synchronization and clock recovery; cross-talk from timing error. E1 example: 8 kHz frames, 32 slots, 8 bits per slot, 2.048 Mbit/s. Some syllabi write TDM(A) for time-division multiple access; TDM is the multiplexing idea, TDMA is multiple access.

figure.aria: One 125 microsecond frame carries four 8-bit channel slots followed by one synchronisation bit, giving 33 bits per frame.

chapters.example: Four 4 kHz signals are sampled at 8 kHz and coded with 8-bit PCM. One synchronisation bit is added per frame. Find frame duration, bits per frame, and bit rate. Answer: Tf = 1/8000 = 125 μs; data bits = 4×8 = 32; total = 33 bits; Rb = 33/125 μs = 264 kbit/s.
chapters.trap: The frame rate equals the sampling rate, not the bit rate. Do not forget sync bits or extra signalling slots when computing Rb. TDM is not FDM; it shares time, not frequency.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.2 PAM and 4.4 PCM; Chapter 4.1 sampling.
chapters.leave: FDM to Unit 2; TDMA/CDMA/OFDMA multiple access to Unit 6; line coding of the multiplexed bit stream to 4.8.

chapters.idea: Line coding maps bits to voltage or current waveforms; NRZ, RZ and Manchester differ in DC content, clock recovery and spectral width.
chapters.depth: Define unipolar, polar and bipolar; NRZ-L, NRZ-I and unipolar NRZ; RZ with return to zero in each bit; Manchester (split-phase, biphase-L) with a transition at every bit centre; mention differential Manchester. Draw waveforms for a given bit sequence. Power spectral density: polar NRZ has sinc²(fTb) with first null at Rb and nonzero DC for unipolar; RZ has first null at 2Rb; Manchester has zero DC and first null at 2Rb. Clock recovery: Manchester is self-synchronising; long NRZ runs lose clock. Bandwidth efficiency: NRZ best, Manchester needs more bandwidth. Some syllabi call Manchester biphase or split-phase coding; differential Manchester is also called CDP. Give the sinc² shape and first null; a full PSD derivation is advanced and only a few universities teach it.

figure.title: Line-code levels for 10110
figure.aria: The table shows bit sequence 10110 and its polar NRZ, RZ and Manchester level patterns, with Manchester using a low-to-high transition for 1 and high-to-low for 0.

chapters.example: A binary sequence 1 0 1 1 0 is sent at 1 kbit/s. Find the bit duration and the first spectral null of polar NRZ, RZ and Manchester. State which code has no DC and self-clocking. Answer: Tb = 1/1000 = 1 ms; first null: NRZ = 1/Tb = 1 kHz; RZ = 2/Tb = 2 kHz; Manchester = 2/Tb = 2 kHz. Manchester has no DC and a transition in every bit, so it is self-clocking. Convention used: 1 = low-to-high, 0 = high-to-low.
chapters.trap: For Manchester the symbol rate is 2Rb because each bit has two half-bit levels; the first null is 2Rb, not Rb. Long runs of 1s or 0s in NRZ cause clock loss; RZ and Manchester restore transitions at a bandwidth cost. Do not call unipolar NRZ DC-free.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.4 PCM bit stream and Chapter 4.7 TDM; Unit 5 pulse shaping and Nyquist bandwidth.
chapters.leave: ISI, eye diagrams and equalization to Unit 5; channel coding to Unit 7; passband modulation to Unit 6.
